title: What were the Freedom Schools?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain the Freedom Schools, community summer schools run in Mississippi in summer 1964 as part of Freedom Summer, organized by SNCC (Student Non-Violent Coordinating Committee) with Robert Moses and Charlie Cobb. Covers the state of segregated sharecropper schools in Mississippi after Brown v. Board of Education, the goal of registering Black voters and challenging the all-white Mississippi delegation at the 1964 Democratic National Convention, recruitment of Northern college volunteers, the disappearance and murder of Goodman, Schwerner and Cheney, the citizenship curriculum (including the Power Structure unit), student newspapers, poetry, the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party, the Mississippi Student Union, Fannie Lou Hamer's testimony interrupted by Lyndon Johnson, violence during the summer, and the later Children's Defense Fund Freedom Schools. Episode also includes banter, a content note about outdated language, and a listener mail segment about due process in Lawrence v. Texas.
topics: Brown v. Board of Education aftermath
Lyndon Johnson Fannie Lou Hamer testimony
listener mail due process Lawrence v. Texas

segments.title: Opening banter and content warning
segments.summary: Hosts joke around, then introduce the Freedom Schools topic and warn that period curriculum uses outdated language including the word Negro.

segments.title: Segregation in Mississippi after Brown v. Board
segments.summary: Background on Brown v. Board of Education, Mississippi's refusal to integrate, unequal per-pupil spending, short sharecropper school years, and the racist content of Black education.

segments.title: Origins of Freedom Summer
segments.summary: Violent response to Black voting agitation in Mississippi; Robert Moses proposes Freedom Summer in 1964 to register voters and force a showdown between federal and local authorities, with white Northern college students as participants; timing tied to the Civil Rights Act and the Democratic National Convention.

segments.title: Purpose and goals of the Freedom Schools
segments.summary: SNCC leader Charlie Cobb proposed the schools in December 1963 for eleventh and twelfth graders, with goals of supplementing high school, broad academic experience, and forming a basis for statewide student action.

segments.title: Volunteer recruitment and white power response
segments.summary: Volunteers recruited through ads, about 700 joined Freedom Summer and about 280 became teachers; they paid their own way and lived with local Black families. White officials treated them as invaders and added highway patrol.

segments.title: Disappearance of Goodman, Schwerner and Cheney
segments.summary: News of the disappearance of CORE workers James Cheney, Michael Schwerner and Andrew Goodman arrived during the Oxford, Ohio orientation; they were later found murdered. The FBI search and Schwerner's widow's comments are discussed.

segments.title: Orientation message and improvised schools
segments.summary: Quote from the Oxford orientation warning teachers they would meet under trees or on lawns; schools grew to about two thousand students across forty one schools, including younger children; one school was burned and classes continued next to the ruins.

segments.title: Citizenship curriculum and student life
segments.summary: Curriculum with reading, writing, arithmetic, science and a citizenship curriculum including the Power Structure unit and Material Things and Soul Things unit. Popular French classes, poetry, student newspapers, typing, and the Free Southern Theater and Pete Seeger.

segments.title: Summer violence and Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party
segments.summary: Statistics on bombings, shootings, assaults and murders during Freedom Summer; Macomb bombings; delegates from the schools formed the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party and wrote a platform, but were refused seating at the Democratic convention, which held a public hearing where Fannie Lou Hamer testified and Lyndon Johnson interrupted with a press conference.

segments.title: Legacy of the Freedom Schools
segments.summary: Mississippi Student Union formed, students desegregated high schools, Ella Baker's leadership idea, Johnson's Civil Rights Act and the shift of the South to Republicans, notable alumni such as Eddie James Carthon, and the Children's Defense Fund revival in the 1980s.

segments.title: Listener mail: due process and Lawrence v. Texas
segments.summary: Listener Keith from Philadelphia explains procedural versus substantive due process in relation to the Lawrence v. Texas decision.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and invite email and social media contact.
